#en:
Caleb keeps saying we should all be asleep by 0200 if we want to be worth anything at 0600, but he is snoring three doors down and I am staring at a wall that will not blink first. So I might as well write.

Sometimes I think the strangest thing about Direwolf is how familiar it feels. Different insignia, cleaner guns, more zero-g time, but the same quiet calculus I grew up with: who is safe to stand next to when the room turns, who you never turn your back on, who will fold when the rounds start skipping off the bulkheads. The brass talk about honor, contracts, chain of command. The real rules live in the seconds between words.

I still remember my first job that was not supposed to lead anywhere. A part-time gig at a dockside supply kiosk, barely more than a closet with a register. Delivering sealed packages to ships, sweeping the grit off the deck, stocking crates of canned protein and discount ammo under flickering lights. I thought it was honest work. Then I noticed how the same three captains always paid in cash, how the scanner never beeped when their packages went out, how the supervisor watched them leave and pretended not to see. I learned the unspoken rules fast: knock twice, never read the label, never ask why there is no manifest.

One of the loaders handed me a bracelet once, thin links of some alloy that caught the light like ice. Said it fell off a crate, nobody would miss it. I knew it had not been bought anywhere near that kiosk. I also knew enough to smile, slip it on, and say thank you. Questions are just another kind of receipt. If you do not generate them, nobody comes looking to reconcile the books.

Direwolf is the same shape at a higher resolution. Nadia plays the loyal professional, and she is, but she also knows who is holding back ammo, which pilots are refueling off the record, which comms tech is being paid by someone else to "accidentally" delay certain transmissions. She never says so directly. She just asks if I have enough spare mags, then glances at the requisition console and raises an eyebrow. Marcus pretends he is all muscle and drills, yet he spends extra time in the sim with the rookies he thinks might actually survive a second contract. He growls about standards, but he does not let them wash out before they learn how to keep their helmet seals clean.

Caleb is different. By-the-book, almost painfully so, but there is a reason the handlers keep putting him on the same teams as me. He believes in the job more than the paycheck, or pretends well enough that it does not matter. When he signs off on an op, he means it. When he hesitates, I listen. Tonight, he hesitated.

We got a briefing packet flagged eyes-only, something to do with "off-grid asset recovery" and a series of derelicts officially written off years ago. The language was almost bureaucratic enough to be boring, but the coordinates formed a pattern I have seen painted in rumor across mess tables and barracks chatter. Cold, distant systems. Half-erased salvage records. Names that only come up in whispers after the third drink. Someone in MAST or close to it has been quietly shuffling certain wrecks toward one shadow ledger, then hiring people like us to make the paperwork match the reality.

No one says it outright, but we all hear the rumors. A lost patrol that followed the wrong beacon. An independent hauler whose transponder data vanished from every registry overnight. An arbitrator who knew the codes too well and disappeared with a hold full of stolen cores. People say there is a place where those ghosts go, a graveyard of hulls too valuable or too embarrassing to leave in the open. Tonight's packet looked like a map with half its lines erased.

I keep wondering if this is another version of that dockside kiosk, just on a system-wide scale: deliver this, do not scan it too closely, do not ask why the manifest is redacted. The difference is that now the packages are starships and the missing receipts look like dead crews.

When I close my eyes I still see one particular hold, years ago, not on a contract but on a station that did not have emergency drills often enough. Fire, alarms warbling out of tune, artificial gravity hiccupping so that debris hung for a second before crashing down again. I was younger, holding on to the only person who had ever tried to keep me off the streets, her breath ragged against my shoulder as bulkheads shuddered and panels tore loose above us. Love and loss twisted together in that stuttering red light, the smell of melting plastic and burnt metal settling into my lungs. I remember thinking, even then, that the rules outside this compartment were already rewriting themselves. That some accountant somewhere would call the whole thing an "incident" and move on.

Maybe that is why I ended up here, in a unit named after a predator that never hunts alone. When the system collapses around you enough times, you stop believing in its protection and start learning to read the gaps. I learned to walk those gaps as a kid, to feel where the power really flows, to see which "temporary measures" quietly become permanent. In Direwolf, that sense is the difference between coming home and being a line item.

So I watch, and I listen. I note which contracts come with too much hazard pay and too little detail. I watch the way the handlers flinch when certain names cross the holo. I hear the whispers that some of our recovery work is not just cleaning up old battles, but erasing proof that they ever happened the way the records say. And I remember the bracelet on my wrist, cold and beautiful, a gift from someone who stole it because that was the only way to survive another day on the docks.

We traced a stray dataslate in the dust back to a pattern of falsified salvage, then listened to a jumpy analyst talk about orders that never made it into the log. Later, in a dead station's quiet, we saw how temporary files about missing ships had been left looping for years, unacknowledged but never erased. The trail from that forgotten kiosk feels a lot shorter now.
zh:
卡莱布一直说要是我们想在六点还有用，就都该在两点前睡着，可他在三扇门外打着鼾，而我盯着一面不肯先眨眼的墙。所以不如写点东西。

有时我觉得恐怖狼最怪的地方是它感觉多熟悉。不同的徽记、更干净的枪、更多的零重力时间，可还是我从小长大的那套安静的算计：房间翻脸时站在谁旁边安全、你永远不能背对谁、子弹开始从舱壁上跳开时谁会垮。长官们谈荣誉、合同、指挥链。真正的规矩活在话与话之间的那些秒里。

我仍记得我第一份本不该通向任何地方的活儿。码头边一家补给小卖部的兼职，比一间带收银机的壁橱大不了多少。给飞船送密封包裹、扫甲板上的沙砾、在闪烁的灯下给一箱箱罐装蛋白和折扣弹药补货。我以为那是诚实的工作。然后我注意到同样的三个船长总用现金付，他们包裹出去时扫描仪从不响，主管看着他们离开却假装没看见。我很快学会了不成文的规矩：敲两下，绝不读标签，绝不问为什么没有清单。

一个装卸工有一次递给我一只手镯，某种合金的细链，折起光来像冰。说它从一只箱子上掉的，没人会想念它。我知道它不是在离那家小卖部很近的地方买来的。我也足够懂事，微笑着戴上，说谢谢。问题只是另一种收据。你不制造它们，就没人来查账。

恐怖狼是同样形状的更高分辨率版本。娜迪亚扮演忠诚的专业人士，她确实是，可她也知道谁在扣着弹药、哪些飞行员在账外加油、哪个通讯技工被别的某人付钱去"意外地"延迟某些传输。她从不直接说。她只是问我备用弹匣够不够，然后瞟一眼请购控制台、抬一抬眉。马库斯假装他全是肌肉和操练，可他会把额外时间花在模拟器里跟那些他认为真能撑过第二份合同的新人一起。他吼着标准，可他不让他们在他学会怎么保持头盔密封干净之前被淘汰。

卡莱布不一样。照章办事，几乎痛苦地如此，可办事员一直把他和我编在同一队是有原因的。他信这份工作胜过信薪水，或者装得足够好，以至于无所谓。当他签核一次行动时，他是认真的。当他犹豫时，我会听。今晚，他犹豫了。

我们拿到一份标着仅限本人查看的简报包，与"脱离电网资产回收"和一连串多年前官方上已注销的弃船有关。措辞官僚到几乎无聊，可那些坐标形成的图案，是我在食堂桌和营房闲聊里以传言形式见过被画出来的。寒冷的、遥远的星系。半擦除的打捞记录。只有喝到第三杯后才在低语里出现的名字。三头同盟里或靠近它的某人一直悄悄把某些残骸推向一本影子账簿，然后雇像我们这样的人去让文书与现实相符。

没人直说，可我们都听到了传言。一支跟着错信标的失落巡逻队。一艘应答器数据一夜之间从每份登记册里消失的独立运货船。一个太懂那些代码、带着满舱偷来的核心消失的仲裁者。人们说有个地方那些鬼会去，一片船壳的墓地，那些船壳太值钱或太尴尬，不能留在明面上。今晚这份数据包看起来像一张半数线条被擦掉的地图。

我一直在想这会不会又是那家码头小卖部的另一个版本，只是放大到星系规模：把这个送过去，别扫描得太细，别问为什么清单被涂黑。区别是如今那些包裹是星舰，而失踪的收据看起来像死掉的船员。

我闭眼时仍看见某一个特定的货舱，多年前，不是在一份合同上，而是在一座没有足够频繁进行应急演练的空间站上。火、警报走调地颤着、人工重力打嗝，让碎片悬了一秒才又砸下来。我更年轻，抓着唯一试图让我离开街头的人，她在我肩上呼吸粗重，舱壁在我们上方震动、面板撕脱。爱与失去在那闪烁的红光里缠在一起，熔化的塑料和烧过的金属的味道沉进我肺里。我记得即便那时我也在想，这个隔舱外的规矩早就在自己改写。某处有个会计会管这整件事叫一次"事件"然后翻篇。

也许那就是我为什么到了这儿，在一支以从不独自狩猎的掠食者命名的部队里。当系统在你周围崩塌足够多次时，你不再相信它的保护，开始学着读那些缺口。我小时候就学会了走那些缺口，感觉权力真正在哪儿流动，看出哪些"临时措施"悄悄变成了永久。在恐怖狼里，那种感觉是回家和变成一行账目之间的区别。

所以我看着，我听着。我记下哪些合同带着太多危险津贴和太少细节。我看办事员在某些名字掠过全息图时畏缩的方式。我听见低语说我们的一些回收工作不只是清理旧战斗，而是抹掉它们曾按记录所称那样发生过的证据。而我想起手腕上那只手镯，冷而美，来自某个偷了它的人，因为那是他在码头上再活一天的唯一方式。

我们在灰尘里追踪到一块游离数据板，追出一个伪造打捞的图案，然后听一个紧张的分析师谈论从未进入日志的命令。后来，在一座死站的安静里，我们看见关于失踪飞船的临时文件被留成循环跑了好几年，未被承认却从未被擦除。从那家被遗忘的小卖部开始的这条痕迹，如今感觉短了很多。

#en:
I can hear the reactor hum bedding down for the off-shift, the way it always does when Deepwater slips a little deeper into the dark. Feels colder tonight, even though environmental says we are well within spec. Rhea swore the air smelled like recycled fear at dinner, which made Jonas laugh until he choked on his stew. I laughed too, but it stuck halfway up my throat and never quite came out. Maybe it is just the way the grav plates kept shuddering on the mid-deck, like the ship is trying to shrug something off.

I should not have been on cargo three after lights, but Darius forgot his toolkit again and begged me to grab it before the Trade Authority inspector logs our next systems ping. So I went, like I always go, because I am the only one who remembers where everyone leaves everything. That is what I tell myself, anyway. The hold was quiet, just the clink of maglocks settling and that slow, hollow creak you only get when a ship is really alone. I almost turned around when I heard voices.

Galen and Rhea, down by the auxiliary console. They did not see me around the crate stack. I know I should have walked away, made some noise so they knew I was there, anything but stand there with my hand over my mouth like some spacer child hiding from ghosts. But I froze. I always thought Galen was just quietly ambitious, the kind of man who knows which side of a ledger to fall on and never makes waves. Hearing him talk in that low, flat voice made the hair on my arms lift.

I could not catch everything, just pieces between the cargo scanner chirps. Payment cleared. Window in the patrol net. No questions from the bosses as long as the manifests match. Rhea asked if he was sure about "the handoff" and he said it was already set, that this route "belongs to other people now" and we just keep our mouths shut and ride it out. The way he said "other people" made my stomach twist, like there was a third ship in the hold with us, listening.

I backed away, bumped into a crate, and nearly dropped Darius's damn toolkit. Galen called out, asked if someone was there, and I forced myself to step around the corner with the most casual smile I could manage. Told them I was just playing errand girl again. Rhea looked like she swallowed a whole asteroid. Galen smiled too easily, asked if I ever sleep, and my cheeks went hot for no good reason. I hate that about myself, the way my face advertises every thought I do not say.

On the walk back I kept replaying it, trying to tell myself it was nothing. Trade Authority runs side deals all the time. Priority cargo, priority clients. Maybe that is all it is. But the way he stood too close to the console when I passed, as if he did not want me to see what was on it, that is not "standard incentive." I know enough smugglers' tricks from Gagarin to recognize the shape of one, even if I pretend otherwise.

Then there was this morning in the galley, which I would erase from my memory if I could. I walked in just as Galen was rinsing his cup, and the ship had this weird half-gravity hiccup while the stabilizers recalibrated. I stumbled, grabbed the counter, and he caught my elbow at the same time. For half a second we were both braced together, his hand warm through the sleeve of my coverall, my hair floating stupidly in my face. He made some joke about me testing the inertial dampeners with my "graceful entrance," and I could not think of anything to say but "I meant to do that."

Who says that? I meant to do that. I replayed it all day, cringing at every angle. Part of me wanted to stay in that stupid almost-embrace and pretend he was just another crew mate teasing me, not someone whispering about handoffs and patrol windows in the dark. Part of me wanted to pull away, march straight to Jonas, and dump everything I heard on the table between us. Instead I mumbled something about shift reports and fled with my coffee sloshing over my hand.

I keep asking myself who I am loyal to. To Deepwater, her logs and her unremarkable corridors. To the Trade Authority, who will absolutely not hesitate to vent a whole crew for stepping out of line, then deny we ever existed. To the faces I see every day, trading bad jokes and good coffee in the galley. Or to the tiny, selfish part of me that wonders if Galen is right, if there is a way to come out of all this with more than a pension and worn-out boots.

Rhea has been quieter since that conversation. She watches Galen when she thinks no one is looking, as if trying to decide whether she is on his side or just near the blast radius. Darius buried himself in maintenance on the external relays, grumbling about how they do not pay him enough to fix old Trade Authority shortcuts. Jonas keeps talking about what he will buy after this run, like spending the credits in his head will guarantee he lives long enough to touch them.

The rumor mill has gone dry, and that is what scares me most. Normally there is always some story about pirates out past Akila or Ryujin making plays in Neon, the usual noise. Lately the stories come in whispers, like the space between systems has teeth, and someone is paying good money to sharpen them. I hear it in the way the dockers on Gagarin spoke too softly when they mentioned our route, in how a bartender on New Atlantis changed the subject as soon as he saw our ship patch.

If I bring this to anyone official, it is my word against Galen's, and he knows how to dress his lies in the right paperwork. If I stay quiet, I am complicit in something I do not understand. And in the middle of all that, there is the part of me that still feels the echo of his hand on my arm and hates myself for it. I do not know if I want him to be innocent or just honest.

For now I will do what I always do: log my shift, double-check the environmental seals, and pretend I do not notice when the course projections shift a few degrees off the standard lanes. But I have started keeping my own copy of the route data, tucked where no one looks. If this goes bad, I want someone, somewhere, to know we did not just vanish. We were steered.
zh:
我能听见反应堆的嗡鸣在为休班沉淀下来，像深水号一点点滑进更深的黑暗时它总是那样。今晚感觉更冷，尽管环境系统说我们完全在规格内。瑞亚赌咒说晚饭时空气闻起来像再循环的恐惧，这让乔纳斯笑得呛住了炖菜。我也笑了，可它卡在我喉咙一半、始终没出来。也许只是中层甲板的重力板一直震颤的方式，像飞船在试图抖掉什么。

熄灯后我不该在 3 号货舱，可达里乌斯又忘了他的工具包，求我在贸易管理局检查员记录我们下次系统探测之前去拿。于是我去了，像我一直去的那样，因为我是唯一记得每个人把每样东西落在哪儿的人。反正我就是这么告诉自己的。货舱很安静，只有磁力锁落定的叮当和那种只有飞船真孤单时才会有的缓慢、空洞的吱嘎。听到声音时我差点转身离开。

盖伦和瑞亚，在辅助控制台旁。他们没看见我在箱堆后面。我知道我该走开、弄出点声响让他们知道我在那儿、做任何事而不是站在那儿用手捂着嘴像某个躲鬼的太空人孩子。可我僵住了。我一直以为盖伦只是安静地有野心，那种知道该倒向账簿哪一边、从不掀波的男人。听他那样低而平板地说话让我手臂上的汗毛竖起。

我没抓全，只是货物扫描仪啁啾之间的一些碎片。付款已结清。巡逻网里的窗口。只要清单对得上，老板们不问问题。瑞亚问他是否确定"那笔交接"，他说已经安排好了，说这条航线"如今属于别人"，我们只管闭嘴、熬过去。他说"别人"的方式让我胃里一拧，像货舱里还有第三艘船跟我们在一起，在听着。

我后退，撞上一只箱子，差点掉了达里乌斯那该死的工具包。盖伦喊出声，问有没有人在那儿，我强迫自己绕出拐角，带着我能挤出的最随意的笑。告诉他们我又在跑腿。瑞亚看起来像吞了一整颗小行星。盖伦笑得太轻易，问我到底睡不睡，我的脸颊没来由地发烫。我讨厌自己这一点，我的脸把我没说出口的每个念头都广而告之。

回去的路上我一直在重放它，试图告诉自己那没什么。贸易管理局一直在搞私下交易。优先货物、优先客户。也许就这些。可当我经过时他站得离控制台太近、像不想让我看见上面是什么的样子，那不是"标准激励"。我从加加林学到的走私贩把戏够多，能认出一个的形状，哪怕我假装不是。

然后还有今早在厨房，那要是我能的话会从记忆里擦掉。我走进去时盖伦正在冲他的杯子，飞船在稳定器重校时打了一个古怪的半重力嗝。我绊了一下，抓住柜台，他同时接住了我的手肘。有那么半秒我们俩一起撑着，他的手透过我连身服的袖子是温的，我的头发愚蠢地在脸前飘着。他开了个玩笑，说我用我"优雅的入场"测试惯性阻尼器，我想不出任何话，只说"我是故意的"。

谁会那么说？我是故意的。我一整天重放它，为每个角度蜷缩。我身上一部分想留在那个蠢蠢的、几乎拥抱的姿势里，假装他只是又一个逗我的船友，而不是某人在黑暗中低语交接和巡逻窗口。我身上一部分想抽开、径直走到乔纳斯那儿、把我听到的一切倒在我们之间的桌上。结果我嘟囔了句关于班次报告的话，端着洒到手背上的咖啡逃走了。

我一直问自己我效忠谁。效忠深水号、她的日志和她不起眼的走廊。效忠贸易管理局，他们绝对会毫不犹豫为一个越线的人抽空整队船员、然后否认我们存在过。效忠我每天见到的面孔，在厨房里交换烂笑话和好咖啡。或者效忠我身上那个微小、自私的部分，它想知道盖伦是不是对的，是否有办法从这一切里带出比一份养老金和破靴子更多的东西。

那次谈话之后瑞亚更安静了。她在以为没人看时看着盖伦，像在试图决定她是站在他那边，还是只是靠近爆炸半径。达里乌斯把自己埋进外部中继站的维护里，嘟囔着他们付他的钱不够修旧贸易管理局的捷径。乔纳斯一直谈这趟之后他要买什么，像在脑子里花掉那些信用币就能保证他活得够久去碰它们。

传言工厂干涸了，而这最让我害怕。通常总有些关于阿基拉外海盗、或龙神在霓虹城布局的故事，那些惯常的噪声。近来故事以低语到来，像星系之间的太空有牙，而有人正花大钱磨利它们。我从加加林码头工提到我们航线时说话太轻的方式里听到它，从新亚特兰蒂斯一个酒保一看见我们的船徽就换话题里听到它。

要是我把这事告诉任何官方，那就是我的话对盖伦的话，而他知道怎么给他的谎言穿上对的文书。要是我保持沉默，我就是我不理解之事的同谋。而在这一切中间，是我身上仍感到他手在我手臂上回响、并为此恨自己的那部分。我不知道我是想让他无辜，还是只是想让他诚实。

眼下我会做我一直做的事：记录我的班次、复核环境密封、假装没注意到航向投影偏出标准航道几度。可我已经开始留自己那份航路数据，藏在一个没人看的地方。要是这变糟，我想让某处的某人知道我们不是就这么消失了。我们是被引导的。
